questions.question: Which phrase best explains the interpretation of sequential compactness?
options: Closed under limits of its convergent sequences only.
Every sequence in it converges, with no subsequence needed.
Closed under limits of subsequences of its sequences.
Each sequence has a convergent subsequence, maybe with limit outside.

questions.question: What is the limit requirement in sequential compactness?
options: The subsequence limit must lie outside the set itself.
The subsequence limit must belong to the same set.
The whole sequence must converge.
The subsequence must diverge.

questions.question: Which set is sequentially compact in $\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\|x\|\le 1\}$
$\mathbb{R}^n$
$(0,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}$
An unbounded open ray such as $(0,\infty)$

questions.question: Why is a finite set sequentially compact in a metric space?
options: Every sequence in it is eventually constant, hence convergent.
Any sequence has a constant subsequence at some point.
It is closed, and every closed set is sequentially compact.
It is bounded, and every bounded set is sequentially compact.

questions.question: In a general metric space $(X,d)$, how are compactness (defined with open covers) and sequential compactness related for a subset $E$?
options: They are equivalent: $E$ is compact if and only if it is sequentially compact.
Compact implies sequentially compact, but not conversely.
Sequentially compact implies compact, but not conversely.
They are equivalent only in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where both mean closed and bounded.

questions.question: Let $E=(0,1]\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric. Which argument correctly decides whether $E$ is sequentially compact?
options: $E$ is not sequentially compact: every subsequence of $(1/i)$ converges to $0$, which is not in $E$.
$E$ is sequentially compact: $(1/i)$ is a sequence in $E$ with a convergent subsequence.
$E$ is sequentially compact: $E$ is bounded, so every sequence in $E$ has a convergent subsequence.
$E$ is not sequentially compact: the sequence $\tfrac{1}{2},1,\tfrac{1}{2},1,\dots$ in $E$ does not converge.

questions.question: Let $E$ be a sequentially compact subset of a metric space $(X,d)$, and let $(x_i)$ be a sequence with every $x_i\in E$ that converges to a point $x\in X$. Must $x$ belong to $E$?
options: No: only some subsequence is guaranteed to converge in $E$, and its limit may differ from $x$.
No: $x$ may lie outside $E$, just as $1/i\to0$ with every $1/i$ in $(0,1]$.
Yes: some subsequence converges to a point of $E$, and every subsequence converges to $x$.
Yes, but only in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where Bolzano-Weierstrass makes $E$ closed.
